articles.title: How to write tool descriptions for AI agents
articles.excerpt: Tool descriptions for AI agents are the part of an MCP server that most people knock out in ten seconds. One sentence, done, on to the interesting code. Yet that sentence decides whether the agent fin…
articles.body: Tool descriptions for AI agents are the part of an MCP server that most people knock out in ten seconds. One sentence, done, on to the interesting code. Yet that sentence decides whether the agent finds your tool at all, whether it calls it with sensible parameters and whether it recovers after an error or gives up. In my article Building an MCP server with TypeScript I only touched on the topic briefly. Here I go deep on tool descriptions for AI agents: What does the model actually see, which rules hold up, and how do you check tool descriptions automatically before an agent trips over them? Our example is a small, made-up bike rental. In short An AI agent picks tools solely from their name, description and input schema; it never sees the code behind them.

articles.title: Tailwind vs UnoCSS vs Panda CSS: Build Times Compared
articles.excerpt: The CSS utility-first landscape has evolved beyond Tailwind. UnoCSS and Panda CSS have emerged as serious contenders, each with different philosophies about how developers should write styles in compo…
articles.body: The CSS utility-first landscape has evolved beyond Tailwind. UnoCSS and Panda CSS have emerged as serious contenders, each with different philosophies about how developers should write styles in component-based frameworks. Rebuilding the same production React dashboard once per framework is the cleanest way to compare developer experience, bundle size, and maintainability. Here is what separates them. Quick Verdict UnoCSS is the best option for new projects in 2026 if you value minimal bundle size (on-demand scanning eliminates unused styles) and customizability. Tailwind CSS 4 remains the safest choice for teams prioritizing documentation depth, community packages, and hiring ease.

articles.title: No Server, No Database, No Accounts: What I Learned Building Browser-Only Tools
articles.excerpt: I got tired of the same routine. const out = await heic2any({ blob: file, toType: "image/jpeg", quality: 0.92 }); // read state on load const q = new URLSearchParams(location.search); if (q.has("princ…
articles.body: I got tired of the same routine. I'd need to convert one HEIC photo, or check a file's EXIF data, or work out a loan payment. I'd land on some converter site, upload the file to a stranger's server, wait, download the result, and then wonder where that file actually went. It bugged me. Most of these jobs don't need a server at all. So I built verystep.com — a growing collection of free utilities that run entirely in the browser. No backend doing the work. No database. No sign-ups. Your files and inputs stay on your device because, well, there's nowhere for them to go. This post is the making-of. The choices, the trade-offs, and a few things I got wrong first. The one rule I started with If a job can be done client-side, it must be done client-side. That sounds simple. It gets strict fast.

articles.title: Logging Service Platforms for Startups: A 4-Stage Checkout Noise Budget
articles.excerpt: A checkout log is useful only if an engineer can tell whether a learner is blocked, how many learners are affected, and what action is safe. For a startup, the best logging service is therefore not th…
articles.body: A checkout log is useful only if an engineer can tell whether a learner is blocked, how many learners are affected, and what action is safe. For a startup, the best logging service is therefore not the one with the longest feature list. It is the one that preserves that decision signal without turning every retry, validation error, and harmless timeout into an incident. My short answer is to start with Logtail for a focused application-logging workload, choose Datadog when logs must sit beside monitoring and APM, and choose Papertrail when a small team wants lightweight search with little operational ceremony.

articles.title: Nobody Hand-Writes Assembly Anymore. Why Are You Still Reviewing 2,000-Line AI Diffs?
articles.excerpt: TL;DR: In 1957, IBM released Fortran, and veteran engineers furiously swore they would never trust machine-generated assembly without manual verification. Today, history is repeating itself. High-leve…
articles.body: TL;DR: In 1957, IBM released Fortran, and veteran engineers furiously swore they would never trust machine-generated assembly without manual verification. Today, history is repeating itself. High-level languages are quietly becoming the new machine code. Staring bloodshot-eyed at a 2,000-line AI git diff isn't rigorous engineering—it's performative security theater. Here is why the old Code Review paradigm is dead, how the "Three Defenses" replace it, and how combining agy (Antigravity CLI) with multi-agent orchestration tools like Polter gives us our sanity back. In 1957, IBM unveiled something that shook the computing world to its core: Fortran . It was the world’s first true high-level programming language. Before Fortran, writing software was an exercise in pure masochism.

articles.title: Secrets Management: Why Your API Keys and Passwords Should Never Live in Your Code
articles.excerpt: Imagine pushing your application to GitHub, only to realize you've accidentally committed your production database password or payment gateway API key. Even if you delete it in the next commit, the da…
articles.body: Imagine pushing your application to GitHub, only to realize you've accidentally committed your production database password or payment gateway API key. Even if you delete it in the next commit, the damage may already be done. This is why Secrets Management is an essential part of building secure applications. What Is Secrets Management? Secrets Management is the process of securely storing, accessing, rotating, and revoking sensitive credentials used by applications. These secrets include: API keys: Credentials used to authenticate requests to external services. Database credentials: Usernames and passwords used to access databases. Encryption keys: Keys used to encrypt and decrypt sensitive information. Signing keys: Keys used to generate and verify cryptographic signatures.

articles.body: Resposta curta O Corpus: Planalto, LexML, ANVISA, BCB é um conjunto estruturado de textos jurídicos oficiais brasileiros — incluindo leis, decretos, resoluções e normas técnicas — integrado por meio de padrões abertos (como o LexML) para viabilizar busca semântica, interoperabilidade e aplicação de guardrails em sistemas de IA regulatória. Ele não é uma base de dados unificada oficial, mas um corpus conceitual adotado por iniciativas de governança de IA no Brasil que dependem de fontes primárias autorizadas. articles.title: Astronomers found a mysterious object beyond Neptune, and it could be a new dwarf planet
articles.excerpt: The Vera Rubin Observatory has discovered a suspected dwarf planet beyond Neptune's orbit. If confirmed, it would be the sixth known dwarf planet in our solar system.
articles.body: The powerful Vera Rubin Observatory has spotted what seems to be a dwarf planet circling the sun in the frigid depths beyond Neptune. The icy object, known as 2026 ED138, is likely between 600 and 1500 kilometers (373 to 972 miles) wide, scientists say. It's therefore probably big enough to be sculpted into a sphere by its own gravity — a key characteristic that separates dwarf planets from asteroids and other small space rocks. And if 2026 ED138 is indeed a dwarf planet, that's a pretty big deal, as astronomers have confirmed just five of them to date: Pluto , Ceres, Eris, Haumea and Makemake . An illustration of the solar system showing the orbital pathway of newly discovered dwarf planet candidate 2026 ED138 (ED138). (Image credit: NSF–DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory/NOIRLab/SLAC/AURA/R.

articles.title: Black holes can split in two — but only if they spin at extreme speeds
articles.excerpt: Scientists have long known that when two black holes collide, they merge to create a more massive black hole. New research suggests that the opposite may happen too: single black holes may split in tw…
articles.body: Scientists have long known that when two black holes collide, they merge to create a more massive black hole. These events are so violent that they set the very fabric of space ringing with ripples called gravitational waves. Now, new research suggests that the opposite may happen, too: single black holes may be able to split in two. But this can only happen if that progenitor black hole is spinning at maximum possible speed. That speed prevents the black holes from immediately falling back on each other. There are physical laws in place that would usually prevent black holes from splitting in two; the team behind this research investigated whether there are conditions in which these laws can be temporarily bypassed.
